titleEn: Wolof greetings that ask after the whole household, one person at a time
facts: A Wolof encounter opens with Salaamaalekum, then Naka nga def? (how are you), answered Maa ngi fi rekk (I am here only).
Greetings continue by asking after each relative in turn, and the asker may repeat the same question for every family member.
Plural and respectful forms exist: Naka ngeen def? addresses a group or an elder household rather than one person.
Dakar speakers mix Wolof and French freely in business, but the greeting sequence itself usually stays in Wolof.
Answering with a problem rather than fine is acceptable; the ritual is about recognition before information.
exampleEn: A young man entering a courtyard in Thies greets each elder separately and stays standing until the oldest replies, because an unanswered greeting would mark the whole family as unwelcoming.
qualificationEn: Greeting length varies sharply between Dakar, Casamance and rural areas; not every Wolof speaker follows the full sequence, and many urban conversations skip the relatives entirely.

titleEn: Sanankuya: the Malian licence to insult your joking cousin
facts: Sanankuya pairs whole clans or ethnic groups, for example Bambara farmers and Bozo fishers, in a relationship where mockery is obligatory rather than offensive.
A joker may demand food, accuse the other of greed or call them a slave's descendant, and the target must laugh rather than retaliate.
The relationship carries obligations: the parties must help at weddings and funerals and must not let a quarrel escalate.
Mali's 1990s democratic transition used sanankuya rhetoric publicly to reconcile northern and southern political elites.
Family names can trigger the relationship on introduction, so a surname carries social expectations before anything else is known.
exampleEn: Two strangers meeting in Bamako discover they are Traore and Diarra; the Traore immediately claims the Diarra owes him a goat, and the scripted insult becomes the reason they exchange phone numbers.
qualificationEn: Not every Malian name or ethnic pairing carries sanankuya, and urban practice is often symbolic. The insults are scripted role-play, never a licence for a visitor to improvise.

titleEn: Three tones, one syllable: how Yoruba pitch separates hand, respect and money
facts: Yoruba marks three pitch levels with acute and grave accents, and the unmarked mid tone is just as contrastive as the others.
Ọwọ́ means hand, ọ̀wọ̀ means respect, and owó means money; the first two share consonants and vowels and differ only in tone.
Tone also does grammar: the pronoun written o means you on one pitch and he or she on another, so pitch carries sentence roles.
Yoruba is written with sub-dots for e, o and s plus tone marks, so keyboards without diacritics force readers to infer from context.
It is one of Nigeria's three national languages and is taught in southwest schools, though English dominates upper secondary.
exampleEn: A Lagos radio presenter writes the letters o-w-o on a whiteboard and asks listeners which word they heard; only the tone and vowel marks tell them whether the sentence concerns a hand, respect or money.
qualificationEn: Tone realisation shifts in fast speech and differs between Yoruba varieties. Written tone marks are often dropped online, so learners relying on text alone miss the contrasts.

titleEn: Nnọọ: the Igbo welcome that is followed by a kola nut, not a question
facts: Nnọọ is the standard welcome, often extended to Nnọọ n'ụlọ (welcome into the house) and answered Daalụ (thank you).
Hospitality begins with kola nut and water; the kola is presented, blessed and shared before business is discussed.
Kola (ọjị) has its own vocabulary of offering and refusal, and turning it down can read as rejecting the household rather than the nut.
Greetings change with the day: Ụtụtụ ọma (good morning), Ehihie ọma (good afternoon) and Mgbede ọma (good evening).
Igbo has many dialects, so welcome words and greetings differ between Onitsha, Nsukka and Owerri, and standard Igbo is largely a school construction.
exampleEn: A visitor to an Owerri home is handed a kola nut before being asked why they came; until the nut is broken and shared, the conversation stays on family, health and the journey.
qualificationEn: Kola presentation is common but not universal, especially in urban or strongly Christian households; some families substitute a prayer and soft drinks, and younger hosts may skip the ritual entirely.

region: Swahili coast (Dar es Salaam, Zanzibar, Mombasa)
titleEn: Shikamoo: the Swahili greeting that lowers the younger speaker
facts: Shikamoo, literally I hold your feet, is addressed to elders and superiors, and the expected reply is Marahaba.
The greeting is taught early enough that Tanzanian children use it before speaking to any older person, including teachers and shopkeepers.
Age rather than rank usually triggers it: an older sibling or a cleaner receives shikamoo, while a peer receives habari or mambo.
Mambo answered with Poa is the informal youth exchange; answering Poa to shikamoo would be a clear register error.
Greetings often come in chains, Hujambo? (are you well) followed by Sijambo (I am well) and then news about the family.
exampleEn: In a Dar es Salaam staffroom a new graduate greets the oldest cleaner with shikamoo before greeting colleagues with mambo; the cleaner answers marahaba and the exchange quietly settles who is junior.
qualificationEn: Usage is stronger on the coast and in Tanzania than in inland Kenya, where habari or sasa may replace it; young urban speakers sometimes shorten or play with the form.

expression.glossEn: I hold your feet (respectful greeting to an elder)

region: Nationwide, strongest in central and western Kenya
titleEn: Harambee: Kenya's word for pulling a project together in one afternoon
facts: Harambee, pull together, names the fundraising meeting where neighbours pledge money aloud, one by one, for school fees, a funeral or a water tank.
It appears on Kenya's coat of arms and was a founding slogan of the independence government in 1963.
Pledges are public and recorded by a committee, and a pledge is a social debt that may be collected years later.
Harambee money built a large share of Kenya's secondary schools and technical institutes, and harambees still pay hospital bills for people in the same ward.
The institution is criticised for pressuring poor households and for turning political favour into a visible donation.
exampleEn: At a Nairobi harambee for a colleague's funeral the MC reads the family's budget, then calls donors by name; a junior clerk pledges a week's salary rather than be seen absent from the community.
qualificationEn: The size, openness and social pressure of harambees vary by region and class; some Kenyans avoid them, and church or mosque collections often replace them in cities.

region: Central and northern highlands (Addis Ababa, Gondar, Mekelle)
titleEn: Erswo and ante: Amharic's polite you that borrows the plural
facts: Amharic distinguishes ante (you, masculine singular) from erswo (polite you), which takes plural verb agreement.
The polite form is used upward in age and rank and by service staff to customers, while parents may still receive ante from their own children.
Agreement follows the pronoun: Erswo endet naweot? (how are you) uses a plural verb form that a singular subject would not take.
Using ante too early can sound either warm or rude depending on the setting, and urban speakers often manage it with titles instead.
Religious and court language keeps a further honorific layer, where plural agreement honours God or a person of high rank.
exampleEn: A young Addis Ababa clerk switches to erswo with a customer twice her age and back to ante with a colleague her own age in the same minute, and neither party notices the grammar shift.
qualificationEn: Usage differs between Amharic, Tigrinya and Oromo and between generations; diaspora Amharic speakers often simplify to one you, and gender also affects which form is polite.

region: Nationwide, especially Kgatleng, Kweneng and Serowe
titleEn: The kgotla: where a Motswana speaks only after the circle is opened
facts: A kgotla is the open meeting place and customary court of a Botswana village, held in a semicircle with the chief or headman at the centre.
Speaking is orchestrated: the meeting opens with prayer, the chair invites speakers in order, and elders are heard before juniors.
Speeches end with Pula (rain), a blessing that is also the national motto and the signal that the point is formally closed.
Decisions are announced from the same circle, and elected ward councillors still use kgotla meetings to report back to voters.
Interrupting a speaker or addressing the chair as an equal rather than through the meeting is a serious breach of procedure.
exampleEn: In a Kweneng kgotla a young man waits through two older speakers before the chair nods at him; he stands, greets the circle with Dumelang, and finishes with Pula.
qualificationEn: Kgotla protocol varies by ethnic group and between rural and urban wards; in Gaborone many disputes go to formal courts, and women's speaking roles have changed unevenly.

region: Nationwide, heaviest in the south and in cities
titleEn: Wetin dey happen: how Nigerian Pidgin compresses a whole conversation
facts: Nigerian Pidgin is a creole spoken by well over a hundred million people, yet it is not an official language and is rarely examined in school.
Its tense system uses particles: dey marks ongoing action, don marks completion and go marks the future, as in I dey go and I don go.
Questions are often made by intonation alone, so You dey come? needs no auxiliary to ask whether someone is coming.
Radio, Nollywood and social media made Pidgin a national lingua franca, and politicians now use it to sound unscripted.
The orthography is unstandardised, so one sentence may appear as wetin dey happen, wetyn de happen or wetin de hapun.
exampleEn: Two traders from different language groups meet at Onitsha main market and settle a price entirely in Pidgin, switching to Igbo only when a third trader joins; both treat Pidgin as neutral ground.
qualificationEn: Pidgin is not uniform: Lagos, Port Harcourt and Warri varieties differ in vocabulary and in how much English they mix, and some educated speakers avoid it in formal settings.

titleEn: Sawubona: the Zulu greeting that says I see you
facts: Sawubona is usually translated I see you or we see you and is addressed to one person; Sanibonani addresses a group.
The reply Yebo, sawubona (yes, I see you) completes the exchange, which acknowledges presence rather than exchanging information.
Greetings often continue with a clan praise name (isithakazelo) and a question such as Uhlala kuphi? (where do you stay).
The word entered South African English through media and is often linked to the ubuntu idea that a person is a person through other people.
Delivery matters: a clipped sawubona to an elder sounds dismissive, so speakers add the clan name or a title.
exampleEn: A Durban nurse greets a patient with sawubona and then a clan name read from the file; the patient relaxes visibly, because being named by clan is a form of recognition rather than small talk.
qualificationEn: Greeting length varies by age, setting and region; isiZulu in Gauteng mixes with English and Sotho languages, and not every Zulu speaker knows the clan names expected of them.

titleEn: Three clicks in one word: Xhosa's borrowed consonants
facts: isiXhosa has three basic click types written c, x and q, plus clusters such as gc, nc and ngc.
The clicks entered Xhosa from Khoisan languages and are now ordinary consonants in everyday words such as cela (to ask).
The name of the language begins with one: isiXhosa uses the lateral x click that English speakers rarely attempt.
Children acquire clicks at the same age as other consonants, so they are not especially hard for first-language speakers.
Writing them required Latin letters plus digraphs, and radio presenters still spell unfamiliar names by click type.
exampleEn: At a Cape Town clinic a receptionist spells a surname by click names, the dental c and the lateral x, because the letters alone do not tell a non-Xhosa speaker where to put the tongue.
qualificationEn: Click inventories and spellings differ among Xhosa, Zulu and Southern Sotho; urban speakers may use English place names instead, and casual speech uses fewer clicks than dictionaries suggest.

region: Nairobi estates and other Kenyan cities
titleEn: Sheng: the Nairobi street code that changes faster than the dictionary
facts: Sheng began in Nairobi's Eastlands in the 1970s as a Swahili base thickened with English, Kikuyu and Luo words.
Its vocabulary turns over quickly: words for money, police and friend are replaced once outsiders learn them.
Matatu crews, radio hosts and musicians spread Sheng nationwide, and it now appears in advertising aimed at under-thirties.
Teachers and parents often treat it as a threat to proper Swahili, while linguists describe it as a register rather than a broken language.
Sheng has no fixed orthography, so the same word may be spelled three ways in one thread of messages.
exampleEn: Two matatu touts in Kasarani negotiate a fare in Sheng, switch to Swahili for a passenger and to English when a traffic officer approaches, running the same exchange in three registers within a minute.
qualificationEn: Sheng is not one code: each estate has its own vocabulary, and rural Kenyans may know only a handful of its words. Claims that it is declining usually describe change, not collapse.

region: Atlas Mountains, Kabylie, Rif and Souss
titleEn: Azul: how Tamazight speakers greet in a language long kept out of school
facts: Azul is the everyday Amazigh greeting in Morocco and Algeria, answered Azul fellawen (hello to you all).
Tamazight is a family of related languages, including Tashelhit, Tarifit, Kabyle and Tuareg, so greetings differ across the Atlas.
Morocco adopted Tifinagh for official use in 2003, while Algerian Amazigh mostly writes in a Latin orthography.
Morocco made Tamazight official in the 2011 constitution, twelve years after it was first allowed into classrooms, and implementation remains uneven.
Choosing azul instead of salam in a mixed setting signals Amazigh belonging rather than a lack of Arabic.
exampleEn: A shopkeeper in Tiznit opens with azul to a customer wearing an Amazigh emblem, then switches to Arabic with the next customer; neither exchange is about language ability.
qualificationEn: Tamazight varieties are not mutually intelligible and the standard taught in Moroccan schools is new; many urban Amazigh speakers greet in Arabic or French and use Tamazight at home.

titleEn: Ya ni: the Egyptian word that means I mean and buys time
facts: Ya ni, literally it means, works as a filler, a hedge, a repair marker and sometimes an ironic shrug.
In Cairo speech it often replaces a pause, keeping the floor without committing to content.
Said twice, ya ni ya ni signals impatience or that the speaker has just stated something obvious.
Egyptian Arabic is a spoken variety distinct from Modern Standard Arabic, and ya ni rarely appears in formal writing.
The same root gives standard Arabic yani (it means), so the word is understood across the Arab world even where the filler is used differently.
exampleEn: A Cairo taxi driver explaining a route uses ya ni four times in one sentence; the passenger hears not vagueness but a claim that the explanation is obvious and the traffic is not the driver's fault.
qualificationEn: Frequency and function vary by class, region and generation; Gulf and Levantine speakers use different fillers, and written Arabic removes ya ni almost entirely.

region: Ashanti, Eastern, Central and Brong-Ahafo regions
titleEn: Kwame, Kofi, Akosua: Ghanaian names that record the day you were born
facts: Akan speakers give a kradin, a soul name, fixed by the day of the week of birth: Kwame for a Saturday-born man, Kofi for Friday, Akosua for Sunday.
The name is not decorative; it carries expectations about character and is used for formal address as well as teasing.
A child also takes names from the father's line and from Christian baptism, so one person can answer to three names in three settings.
The system travelled with the transatlantic slave trade, and day names survive among Afro-Caribbean and African American families.
Day names appear on official documents, and the order of names on a Ghanaian passport can confuse foreign officials.
exampleEn: Two Ghanaian colleagues meeting for the first time in Accra ask each other's day names before their job titles; discovering both are Yaa turns the meeting into sibling-like teasing.
qualificationEn: The system is Akan and closely related Fante practice, not universal in Ghana; Ewe, Ga and Dagomba communities name differently, and Christian names often take precedence.

expression.glossEn: female name for a Sunday-born child

titleEn: Alliteration instead of rhyme: how Somali poetry is built to be remembered
facts: Somali poetry uses alliteration of one consonant through an entire poem as its main structural device rather than end rhyme.
Genres are ranked: the gabay is the long classical form, while buraanbur is a women's genre with a different rhythm and performance setting.
Poems travel by radio and cassette and have settled disputes, because a well-known poem can name the cost of continued fighting.
Poetry is ordinary competence rather than a specialist art, and speakers quote lines in conversation to make an argument.
Somali adopted a Latin orthography only in 1972, and poetry preserved metres that the written language had to catch up with.
exampleEn: A Mogadishu elder settling a land dispute quotes four lines of a gabay whose repeated consonant carries the argument; the parties recognise the poem before they agree with its conclusion.
qualificationEn: Not all Somali speakers share one poetic canon, and diaspora youth often meet the gabay online rather than by recitation; genres and dialect vary between Somalia, Djibouti and the Ogaden.

region: Nationwide, strongest in offices and service work
titleEn: Otsukaresama desu: the Japanese office phrase that thanks you for existing at work
facts: Otsukaresama desu is said when passing a colleague, at the end of a meeting and when leaving the office; it thanks the other person for their effort rather than for a result.
It belongs to keigo, the honorific register with three layers: sonkeigo (respectful), kenjogo (humble) and teineigo (polite).
A superior may say gokurosama downward to a subordinate, but a junior should not use it upward; the direction of the phrase is grammaticalised.
Email openings often use osewa ni natte orimasu, the humble form of thank you for your support, to the same end.
The phrase has no one-word English equivalent, which is why subtitles usually leave it as a greeting or drop it.
exampleEn: Two colleagues pass in a Tokyo corridor at 6.55 p.m.; both say otsukaresama desu, though one is arriving for the night shift and the other has not yet done anything that day.
qualificationEn: Keigo depth varies by industry, age and company; many workplaces speak casually internally, and excessive formality between close colleagues can sound ironic.

expression.glossEn: thank you for your hard work / well done

titleEn: Aizuchi: the Japanese nods and hai that mean I am listening, not I agree
facts: Aizuchi are the backchannel responses, such as hai, e and so desu ne, that a listener inserts every few seconds.
They signal attention and comprehension rather than agreement, and Japanese speakers may say hai while preparing to disagree.
Frequent aizuchi are expected; a silent listener can seem cold, while a non-Japanese listener's silence may read as inattention.
Business phone calls require audible backchannels because the other party cannot see the listener at all.
Research on aizuchi describes it as cooperative listenership, with responses timed to the speaker's phrases rather than to the end of a turn.
exampleEn: On a Tokyo conference call the Osaka client says hai, hai every few sentences; the foreign supplier hears consent, but the client later disputes the terms, because hai was the sound of listening.
qualificationEn: Aizuchi frequency differs by dialect and individual; Kansai speakers often backchannel more densely, and long residence abroad reshapes the habit. It is a convention, not a personality test.

expression.glossEn: that is so, isn't it (listening response)

titleEn: Banmal and jondaenmal: Korean's two speech worlds
facts: Korean verbs conjugate for politeness and for the relationship between speaker and listener; banmal is the casual style and jondaenmal the polite one.
The haeyo style is polite but not formal, while hamnida is the formal style used in news, the army and presentations.
Switching to banmal is a social event: someone must offer it with uri mal noeulkkayo? (shall we drop the formal speech), and refusing keeps distance.
Age sets the default, and even a one-year gap usually decides who speaks casually first.
Historical speech levels have contracted, and modern Korean uses about four productively although grammar books list more.
exampleEn: Two university freshmen born in the same year but different months negotiate banmal over coffee; the older offers, the younger hesitates, and the decision is still being tested a week later.
qualificationEn: Workplaces vary: some insist on formal style regardless of age, and K-pop and online communities have normalised banmal between strangers of similar age. Regional and generational norms differ.

expression.glossEn: Shall we switch to casual speech?

titleEn: Mafan ni le: the Chinese phrase that turns a request into a debt
facts: Mafan ni le, roughly I have put you to trouble, is said before and after asking a favour, acknowledging the other person's effort.
Guanxi names the network of reciprocal obligations: a favour creates a debt repaid later, often in a different currency such as a contact, a meal or a job lead.
Refusing is usually done by citing difficulty rather than saying no, and wo jinliang (I will try my best) can be a soft refusal.
Gifts and offers are often declined twice before being accepted, so immediate acceptance can read as greed rather than enthusiasm.
WeChat has formalised guanxi maintenance, with red packets, group chats and likes acting as low-cost reciprocity.
exampleEn: A Shanghai project manager asks a former classmate to introduce a supplier, opening with mafan ni le and closing with a dinner invitation; the dinner is not social, it is the first instalment of repayment.
qualificationEn: Younger urban Chinese increasingly criticise guanxi as corrupt and prefer explicit contracts; regional and generational differences are large, and northern and southern business styles differ.

expression.glossEn: sorry to trouble you / thanks for the favour

titleEn: Add oil: the Cantonese cheer that went global
facts: The characters for add oil are read ga yau in Cantonese and jiayou in Mandarin, and mean keep going or you can do it.
The phrase is shouted at athletes, typed at students and printed on banners, and it travelled into English during the 2010s as add oil.
Cantonese keeps older vocabulary and a full tone system, and many spoken words differ from Mandarin even where the written character is identical.
Hong Kong writes Standard Written Chinese, so a Cantonese sentence is often written in Mandarin grammar and then read aloud in Cantonese.
Add oil entered the Oxford English Dictionary in 2018 as a Hong Kong English expression.
exampleEn: A Hong Kong student writing a final exam receives a sticker of a petrol pump from her mother; the characters never appear, but the message is unambiguous.
qualificationEn: Cantonese and Mandarin are not mutually intelligible in speech; mainland usage of the phrase is Mandarin, and the English loan is specifically Hong Kong. Political associations of the phrase shift with context.

region: Hindi belt: Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh
titleEn: Aap, tum, tu: Hindi's three ways to say you
facts: Aap is the respectful you and takes plural agreement, tum is familiar and tu is intimate or insulting depending on context and tone.
The respect particle ji attaches to names and answers: Gandhi ji, haan ji (yes, sir or madam), Namaste ji.
A parent may use tum with a child while the child must use aap with the parent, so the pronoun indexes direction of respect rather than distance.
Verbs agree with the chosen form: aap kaise hain? versus tum kaise ho? are the same question in two social registers.
In north Indian offices, aap between equals can create distance, and colleagues deliberately switch to tum to signal friendship.
exampleEn: A Delhi intern addresses her manager with aap for two months, then says tum by accident; both laugh, and the manager reads it as the relationship moving rather than as a slip.
qualificationEn: Usage varies by region, gender and generation; Bhojpuri and Awadhi speakers use different pronouns, and Hindi as spoken in Mumbai is heavily mixed with Marathi and English.

region: North India, especially Punjab, Haryana and Delhi
titleEn: Jugaad: the Hindi word for the workaround that becomes a business model
facts: Jugaad names a low-cost improvisation: a motorbike engine strapped to a cart, a rooftop cooler rebuilt from a fridge, a workaround that works once.
The word appears in Punjabi and Hindi, and its origin is debated among speakers and lexicographers.
Management writers turned jugaad into a theory of frugal innovation after cheap cars and dialysis machines were described with it.
It carries a double edge: praise for resourcefulness and criticism for cutting corners, so calling a product jugaad can be an insult.
The makeshift motorised cart also called a jugaad is banned on many Indian roads for safety reasons, which captures the tension exactly.
exampleEn: A Rajasthan farmer builds an irrigation pump from a diesel engine, a bicycle frame and a car radiator; it waters two fields for a season and is never repaired, because it was never designed to be.
qualificationEn: Jugaad is a north Indian term; Tamil, Bengali and Marathi have different words for improvisation, and middle-class Indians often use jugaad ironically about corruption or shoddy work.

region: Urban India, especially Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru
titleEn: Hinglish: switching languages mid-sentence as the normal way to speak
facts: Hinglish mixes Hindi grammar with English vocabulary, as in mera phone kharab ho gaya hai (my phone has stopped working), and it is the default register in urban advertising.
Switching happens at clause boundaries rather than randomly: speakers move between narrative and technical content by changing language.
The mixture is class-marked: English-heavy Hinglish signals education, while Hindi-heavy speech signals local belonging.
Bollywood scripts have used Hinglish since the 1990s, and streaming platforms now subtitle it as a variety in its own right.
Parents and teachers police pure Hindi or pure English even though the mixed register is what most urban speakers actually use.
exampleEn: A Mumbai call-centre worker greets a customer in English, explains the bill in Hindi and switches back to English for the complaint number; the customer never notices, because Hinglish is the expected register.
qualificationEn: Hinglish is not one variety: Bengaluru mixing includes Kannada, and Marathi-English and Tamil-English patterns differ. It is largely urban and middle-class rather than a national code.
