expression.transliteration: mera phone kharab ho gaya hai

titleEn: Tehzeeb: the Urdu manners that turn a request into an apology
facts: Urdu politeness uses honorific titles such as janab, sahib and muhtaram, and plural verbs for a single addressee.
A request is often framed as an imposition, with takleef to nahi hogi? (will it not trouble you?) coming before the actual ask.
Tehzeeb names cultivated manners, and it is judged through speech: softness, indirectness and never refusing outright.
A refusal is typically built as main koshish karunga (I will try) or a delay, so that no is inferred rather than heard.
Urdu and Hindi are largely the same spoken language with different scripts and formal vocabularies, and everyday conversation crosses the border easily.
exampleEn: A Lahore host asks three times whether a guest wants more tea; the guest declines twice and accepts on the third, because refusing all three would mean the host's hospitality failed.
qualificationEn: Tehzeeb is an urban and classed ideal rather than a description of all Pakistanis; Punjabi, Sindhi and Pashto speakers have their own courtesy formulas, and younger Pakistanis mix English into the same register.

expression.glossEn: Will it not trouble you? (May I ask a favour?)

titleEn: Apni, tumi, tui: Bengali's three doors into you
facts: Bengali marks the addressee on the verb at three levels: apni (formal), tumi (familiar) and tui (intimate or contemptuous).
The verb changes with each: apni kemon achen?, tumi kemon acho? and tui kemon achis? ask the same question in three social keys.
Using tui with a stranger is a provocation, while using it with a close friend is warmth; the same word does opposite work.
Elders receive apni even from adult relatives, spouses usually use tumi, and parents may switch to tui when angry.
The three-way pattern is shared with Hindi and other Indo-Aryan languages, but Bengali makes all three levels grammatical through distinct verb endings.
exampleEn: On a Kolkata campus a professor uses apni with a colleague, tumi with a doctoral student and tui with the man who has swept the corridor for twenty years, and the last one is affection rather than contempt.
qualificationEn: Dhaka and Kolkata usage differ; Bangladeshi Bengali uses apni more broadly, and diaspora families often lose tui except in jokes. Verb forms also vary by dialect.

region: Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and northern Sri Lanka
titleEn: Tamil's two registers: the written sentence nobody says aloud
facts: Tamil has a sharp diglossia, and literary Tamil differs from spoken Tamil in verb endings, pronouns and vocabulary.
A written sentence such as nan varugiren (I am coming) is spoken as nan varren, with a different verb ending entirely.
Newsreaders and films occupy different points on the scale: bulletins use literary Tamil, dialogue uses spoken Tamil, and audiences accept both as Tamil.
The split is old, with Sangam-era poetry and modern speech separated by two millennia of change, and political movements have repeatedly tried to purify the written form.
Sri Lankan Tamil and Indian Tamil are close in writing but differ in spoken vocabulary and intonation.
exampleEn: A Chennai student writes a letter to her grandmother in literary Tamil and then phones her in spoken Tamil; the same news takes two shapes because she never says the written forms aloud.
qualificationEn: Diglossia is strongest in formal contexts; Tamil television has popularised intermediate registers, and diaspora schools teach the literary form, so children speak one Tamil and read another.

titleEn: Kreng jai: the Thai reluctance that keeps everyone's options open
facts: Kreng jai describes not imposing: not asking for a lift, not finishing the last dish, not saying what you want so the other person need not refuse.
It is enacted in small refusals, where a second helping is declined before being accepted and a host offers more than once.
The particle system carries status, with khrap ending polite sentences for male speakers and kha for female speakers.
A direct no can be heard as an attack, so refusal is built as mai khoi saduak (not very convenient) or a silent delay.
Kreng jai works upward and downward, but juniors are expected to show it more, which makes workplace feedback indirect.
exampleEn: A Bangkok intern offered work she cannot finish says sorry and asks for a new deadline instead of refusing, and her manager hears the refusal anyway.
qualificationEn: Kreng jai is a norm rather than a personality: urban Thais in tech and international firms often prefer directness, and Chinese-Thai and southern Muslim communities differ.

expression.glossEn: to feel considerate / reluctant to impose

titleEn: Anh, em, chi: Vietnamese turns pronouns into a family tree
facts: Vietnamese second-person pronouns are kinship terms: anh (older brother), chi (older sister), em (younger sibling) and ong or ba for grandparents.
Choosing one assigns a relative age and gender, and the pair must be reciprocal: if I am your em, you are my anh.
Da is the respectful acknowledgement that opens an answer to an elder, functioning as yes and as a signal of deference at once.
Ban is the neutral peer pronoun, a twentieth-century standard spread by schooling and media.
A shop assistant and a customer who look the same age still negotiate pronouns for a few seconds before continuing.
exampleEn: Two strangers on a Vietnamese train spend the first minute estimating each other's age; the older becomes chi and the younger em, and the rest of the journey runs inside those roles.
qualificationEn: Southern and northern usage differ; the neutral ban is spreading among urban youth, and workplace pronouns are sometimes left vague to avoid committing to a hierarchy.

titleEn: Ngoko and krama: Javanese that changes with the person you face
facts: Javanese has three main speech levels, ngoko (intimate), madya (middle) and krama (deferential), with separate vocabulary for the same ideas.
The word for house is omah in ngoko and griya in krama, and a whole dictionary of everyday words has parallel forms.
Levels are triggered by status, age and familiarity, and a speaker can shift mid-conversation when a new person joins.
Krama survives strongly in Yogyakarta and Surakarta, where court traditions and school curricula reinforce it.
Many young urban Javanese speak a mixed register, and language surveys record declining krama use in cities.
exampleEn: A Yogyakarta student speaks ngoko to her brother until an older neighbour arrives, then stays in krama until the neighbour leaves, and nobody comments on the switch.
qualificationEn: Level use varies sharply between cities and villages and is generational; many families use ngoko at home and krama only with older strangers, while Indonesian increasingly replaces both in public life.

titleEn: Po and opo: the Filipino respect words that no sentence can omit
facts: Po is a politeness particle placed after phrases, and opo is the respectful yes, both used with elders, strangers and superiors.
The particle is optional in grammar but not in manners, and dropping it with an older person reads as rudeness.
Kuya (older brother) and ate (older sister) address strangers and colleagues as kin, including supervisors in service work.
The mano gesture, taking an elder's hand to the forehead, survives in families and is usually combined with opo.
English and Tagalog mix in Taglish, but the respect particles usually stay Tagalog, giving sentences such as Yes po, I understand po.
exampleEn: A Manila call-centre agent speaking flawless English still says yes po to a Filipino caller, and the caller's tone softens immediately, because the particle does work the accent cannot.
qualificationEn: Tagalog is the base of Filipino but not everyone's first language; Cebuano and Ilocano have different respect systems, and younger urban speakers sometimes use po playfully.

titleEn: Can lah: the Singlish particles that adjust a sentence's mood
facts: Singlish particles carry stance: lah softens or asserts, leh signals a mild complaint, meh marks disbelief and sia adds emphasis.
Can and cannot are complete answers, and reduplicated verbs intensify the sense, as in wait wait wait or big big.
Syntax drops subjects and articles under Chinese and Malay influence, so Go where? replaces Where are you going?.
The Speak Good English Movement has campaigned against Singlish since 2000, while Singlish remains a marker of national identity.
Singlish is used between locals and avoided with tourists, which makes it a boundary marker rather than a default.
exampleEn: A Singaporean colleague replies can lah, but later ah to a request; the Standard English equivalent would be three sentences, and the particle order still tells you the answer is yes.
qualificationEn: Singlish varies by ethnic background, age and education; many Singaporeans switch to Standard English in writing and to Singlish in hawker centres, and the boundary is about identity, not ability.

region: Nationwide, especially southern and central Sri Lanka
titleEn: Ayubowan: the Sinhala greeting that wishes you long life
facts: Ayubowan means may you live long and serves as hello, goodbye and welcome at once.
The reply is the same word, so a greeting exchange between two people is symmetrical.
The gesture matters as much as the word: palms together at the chest with a slight bow, used with elders and monks.
Sinhala marks respect through verb endings and pronouns, with oba and oya forming a polite and familiar pair.
The greeting is shared by Sinhala Buddhists and used in official settings, while Sri Lankan Tamils greet with vankkam.
exampleEn: A Colombo office lift fills with ayubowan as each person enters; nobody speaks again until the ground floor, but everyone has been acknowledged.
qualificationEn: The word's Buddhist resonance means some Tamil and Muslim Sri Lankans prefer other greetings; in mixed workplaces hello is common, and the palms-together gesture varies by setting.

expression.glossEn: may you live long (hello and goodbye)

titleEn: Khanubhayo: how Nepali conjugates respect into the verb
facts: Nepali marks politeness on the verb, so khayo (he ate) and khanubhayo (he ate, honorific) describe the same act for different people.
The honorific form applies to the subject rather than the listener, so a sentence can honour someone who is not in the room.
Tapaim is the respectful you, timi familiar and ta intimate or insulting, and each brings its own verb agreement.
The system draws on the same Indo-Aryan machinery as Hindi and Bengali, but Nepali extends honorific verbs further than its neighbours.
In Kathmandu, honorific verbs are expected with in-laws and teachers, and using the plain form can be remembered for years.
exampleEn: A Kathmandu student answering a question about an absent teacher uses honorific verbs throughout, because the grammar of respect follows the person being discussed, not the listener.
qualificationEn: Hill and Terai usage differ, and Nepali spoken in Darjeeling or Sikkim follows Indian patterns; Maithili and Bhojpuri speakers in the Terai have their own honorific systems.

titleEn: Sain baina uu and the Mongolian oo that keeps a story going
facts: Sain baina uu (are you well) is the standard greeting, answered sain, sain or sain baina.
Listeners use oo and tiim as backchannels, often drawn out to show attention during a long account.
Mongolian vowel harmony makes suffixes alternate with the word's vowels, so one ending has several correct spellings in Cyrillic.
Mongolian Cyrillic replaced the traditional vertical script in 1941, and the traditional script is now returning to official use alongside it.
Vowel length carries meaning, and a short or long vowel can change a word rather than merely colour an accent.
exampleEn: A herder explaining a hard winter pauses for oo every few sentences; the visiting researcher's silence reads as inattention, while her own English mm-hm does not feel like the right shape of listening.
qualificationEn: Backchannel patterns differ between generations and between Mongolia and Inner Mongolia in China; Russian loanwords are common in Ulaanbaatar speech but rare on the steppe.

region: Nationwide, strongest in Tehran, Isfahan and Shiraz
titleEn: Taarof: the Iranian ritual of refusing what you want
facts: Taarof is the etiquette of offering and refusing: a shopkeeper says naqabel (not worthy of you) and waves away payment while the buyer insists on paying.
It structures ordinary exchanges, including who takes the best seat, the last piece of fruit and the right of way at a doorway.
Declining once is routine, and the third refusal is usually where the real answer lies.
Khahesh mikonam answers thanks and also softens a request, so the same phrase covers please and you are welcome.
The system traps foreigners, who take the first refusal at face value and then appear rude when they insist or greedy when they accept.
exampleEn: A Tehran taxi driver refuses the fare three times; the passenger keeps offering, and both are satisfied when the money is finally left on the seat, because the fare was never in doubt, only the ritual.
qualificationEn: Taarof is not uniform: younger Iranians and diaspora families practise a shortened version, and in business settings the ritual is explicitly adapted or dropped to avoid confusion.

expression.glossEn: you are welcome / please, do not trouble yourself

titleEn: Inshallah: the phrase that commits the future to God and the present to flexibility
facts: In sha Allah, if God wills, follows almost any statement about the future, from a meeting time to a wedding invitation.
It marks humility in Islamic practice: the Quran instructs believers to say it rather than assert what tomorrow will bring.
In everyday use it ranges from sincere to sceptical, and a repeated inshallah can signal that a promise is unlikely to be kept.
The phrase travels with Arabic influence into Turkish insallah, Malay insyaallah and Persian enshallah.
A time confirmed with the phrase is meant sincerely, but people who need certainty usually ask again closer to the date.
exampleEn: A Cairo shop owner says inshallah when promising a delivery on Thursday; the customer comes on Saturday and is not surprised, because the promise was about intention rather than scheduling.
qualificationEn: Usage varies enormously by country, class and religiosity; secular Arabic speakers may use it as a habit rather than a theological statement, and a businessman planning a flight still checks the schedule.

titleEn: Kolay gelsin: the Turkish blessing for whoever happens to be working
facts: Kolay gelsin, may it come easy, is said to anyone visibly working: a waiter, a cleaner, a farmer or a colleague at a desk.
It is neither a greeting nor a thank-you; it acknowledges effort without implying that the speaker wants anything.
Eline saglik (health to your hands) is said to a cook after a meal and to a hairdresser or tailor after their work.
Hos geldiniz welcomes a visitor and gule gule sends them off, and the answer to the welcome is hos bulduk.
The pattern is shared across Turkic and neighbouring languages, from Azerbaijani kolay gelsin to Balkan Turkish usage.
exampleEn: A man walking past a mechanic lying under a car says kolay gelsin without stopping; the mechanic grunts sag ol from the floor, and neither expects the exchange to become a conversation.
qualificationEn: The phrase is widespread but not exclusively Turkish, as Azerbaijani and some Balkan varieties share it; urban speakers often deliver a shortened version as a passing password rather than a genuine blessing.

expression.glossEn: may it be easy (said to someone working)

titleEn: Salemetsiz be: Kazakh between two alphabets and two languages
facts: Salemetsiz be is the formal Kazakh hello, while the shorter Salem is used with equals and friends.
Kazakhstan is bilingual in practice: Kazakh is the state language and Russian the language of interethnic communication, and most urban Kazakhs code-switch daily.
Kazakh moved from Arabic to Latin to Cyrillic in the twentieth century and is now under a decade-long plan to return to Latin, a change that divides generations.
Kazakh has vowels absent from Russian, written in Cyrillic with letters such as a with a bow, o with a bar and u with a straight line.
Language choice is political: young Kazakhs in Almaty increasingly speak Kazakh at work, while northern cities remain Russian-dominant.
exampleEn: Two colleagues in an Almaty office start a meeting in Russian, switch to Kazakh when the manager joins and return to Russian for the technical discussion, because the vocabulary arrived in Russian.
qualificationEn: Language use differs sharply between north and south and between city and countryside; census self-reports overstate spoken Kazakh, and the Latin transition has been postponed more than once.

titleEn: Melmastia: the Pashtun code that makes a guest untouchable
facts: Melmastia is hospitality as obligation: a guest must be fed and protected even if he is an enemy of the host's family.
Nanawatai is the right to seek asylum by entering a house and asking for refuge, and the host is bound to grant it.
Badal is reciprocity and retribution: favours are returned, and wrongs are avenged unless a council of elders settles them.
Pashtunwali is customary law rather than scripture, though it is often described in religious language, and tribal councils apply it unevenly.
The guest rule has practical consequences, because a rural family will spend beyond its means to feed a visitor rather than lose honour.
exampleEn: A stranger whose car breaks down is taken in for the night by a family in the Khyber hills; the host refuses payment the next morning and the guest leaves a gift instead, because the debt cannot be settled directly.
qualificationEn: Pashtunwali is a regional and tribal code, not a national law; urban Pashtuns, Pashtuns in Karachi and the diaspora often observe it symbolically, and women's roles within it are contested and changing.

titleEn: U and Daw: Burmese honorifics that stand where a surname would be
facts: Burmese names have no family name, so U (roughly Mr) and Daw (roughly Mrs) precede an adult personal name, as in U Thant or Daw Aung San Suu Kyi.
Ko and Ma are used before the names of younger men and women, and Maung and Thu appear in other registers and in formal documents.
The honorific is often mistaken abroad for a first name, so the same person is indexed as Thant in one database and U Thant in another.
Polite sentences end with particles that differ by speaker gender, khinbya for men and shin for women, and the pronouns for I are themselves humble forms.
Because names are chosen for meaning rather than inherited, two siblings can share no element of their names at all.
exampleEn: A foreign NGO worker writing to a Burmese official avoids the surname that does not exist and puts U before the name; addressing him as Mr Thant would be understood but marks the writer as an outsider.
qualificationEn: Honorific choices depend on age and setting, and Burmese in exile uses different conventions; Shan, Karen and Chin communities inside Myanmar have their own address systems.

expression.original: ကျေးဇူးတင်ပါတယ်
expression.language: မြန်မာဘာသာ (Burmese)

titleEn: A language brought back to the dinner table: Hebrew's revival
facts: Hebrew was revived as a spoken language from the late nineteenth century, led by Eliezer Ben-Yehuda, after nearly two millennia of mainly liturgical use.
Modern life required new words, so electricity reused an ancient biblical term and computer was coined from a root meaning to think or calculate.
Hebrew builds most words from three-consonant roots, so every new coinage has to fit a pattern that speakers already recognise.
Modern Hebrew has no single polite you, and politeness is carried by bevakasha (please, you are welcome) plus intonation and register.
Arabic is an official language in Israel and Hebrew borrows from it: yalla (come on), sababa (great) and walla (really) are ordinary Hebrew.
exampleEn: An Israeli family argues about dinner plans with yalla and sababa, words borrowed from Arabic, in a language that had no native speakers a hundred and fifty years ago.
qualificationEn: Revival is often oversimplified: Hebrew never stopped being read and written, and the spoken standard drew on Sephardi pronunciation while Yiddish shaped accent and idiom. Haredi and Arab communities use Hebrew differently.

region: Nationwide, strongest in offices and among neighbours
titleEn: Duzen and siezen: the German moment when a stranger becomes a du
facts: German splits the second person between du (familiar) and Sie (formal, grammatically plural), and the choice is not optional small talk.
Colleagues who have worked together for years may still use Sie, while a neighbour you have never met may offer du on the stairs.
The switch is normally proposed by the older or senior person, often with Wollen wir uns duzen? (shall we use du), and refusal is possible.
Verbs and pronouns must agree: Sie kommen and du kommst belong to the same sentence pattern but different social worlds.
East German and southern working-class settings often use du earlier than northern professional ones, and younger Germans switch faster than their parents did.
exampleEn: At a Bonn office Christmas party a manager says we can duzen to a new hire after two months; the hire answers with du immediately, then reverts to Sie the next morning and is gently corrected.
qualificationEn: There is no national rule: companies, regions and age groups differ sharply, and tourists who default to Sie are rarely wrong while learners who default to du often are.

expression.glossEn: Shall we switch to du with each other?

titleEn: Kaixo: Basque greets in a language that has no living relatives
facts: Kaixo is the everyday Basque hello, and agur is goodbye, used with strangers, elders or at the end of the night.
Basque is a language isolate with no demonstrable relatives, and its grammar uses ergative case, so the subject of a transitive verb takes a different ending.
The familiar you is hi, used with close friends and children, while zu is the general polite form and zuek the plural.
Basque survived in mountain valleys and farmhouses where Latin-based languages dominated the towns, and the coastal dialects differ markedly.
The standardised euskara batua was created in the 1960s and is now taught in schools, though older rural speakers still speak local varieties.
exampleEn: In a San Sebastian bar a regular greets the barman with kaixo and a customer he does not know with egun on (good morning), because kaixo presupposes a relationship that the second greeting does not.
qualificationEn: Basque use is strongest in Gipuzkoa and coastal Bizkaia, weaker in Navarre and France; younger speakers are heavily bilingual, and batua can feel bookish to older rural speakers.

titleEn: Gezellig: the Dutch word for a room that is going well
facts: Gezellig applies to situations rather than objects: a cafe, an evening or a visit can be gezellig, and a nice chair cannot.
It combines cosiness with social ease, and the noun gezelligheid names the quality itself rather than any specific activity.
The word is used as an adjective, an adverb and a compliment, and calling a party niet gezellig is a serious verdict delivered mildly.
Dutch social life treats shared time as something to be actively produced, and gezellig is the success condition of that effort.
The same root gives gezelschap (company), which links the word to the idea of being in company rather than being comfortable.
exampleEn: A Dutch colleague declines a loud bar and suggests a small living room with coffee; when asked why, she says simply that it will be more gezellig, and everyone understands the whole evening in one word.
qualificationEn: Gezellig is a norm as much as a feeling, and some Dutch people find the pressure to produce it tiring; Flemish Dutch uses the word slightly differently, and tourists often overuse it.

titleEn: Hygge: the Danish word for deliberately lowering the room's temperature of excitement
facts: Hygge names a calm, safe togetherness, usually indoors, usually with low light, food and no schedule.
It is a verb as well as a noun in practice, and Danes talk about hygge sig (to hygge oneself) as an activity to be arranged.
Social rules apply: loud arguments, phones and work talk can break the atmosphere, and a guest who brings nothing may still be asked to contribute a story.
The word entered global lifestyle publishing in the 2010s, which Danes often describe as a misunderstanding of an ordinary evening.
Hygge is linked to Danish social trust and to the long dark winters, though the connection is a national explanation rather than a proven cause.
exampleEn: A Copenhagen family cancels dinner plans because of rain and stays in with candles, bread and a board game, calling the evening hygge even though nothing was planned as special.
qualificationEn: Hygge is a national self-description rather than a uniform practice; younger Danes mock its commercialisation, and immigrant and working-class households may not recognise the middle-class version.

titleEn: The du reform: how Sweden abolished titles in a decade
facts: Until the 1960s Swedes addressed superiors in the third person (Would the director like coffee?) rather than with du or ni.
The du-reformen of the late 1960s made du the default in almost every setting, pushed by broadcasters, unions and an expanding public sector.
Within about a decade the old title system collapsed, and today addressing a Swedish manager or professor as ni sounds distant or archaic.
The reform was part of a wider democratisation of Swedish workplaces, and it coincided with the expansion of the welfare state.
Finnish and Norwegian developed differently, so Swedish du is a recent choice rather than an ancient egalitarian tradition.
exampleEn: A Stockholm student emails a professor with du and the first name, then apologises when writing in English because English has no equivalent switch and the email suddenly feels presumptuous.
qualificationEn: Du is default but not universal: service staff sometimes use ni to older customers, and Swedish-speaking Finns follow different norms. The reform was a media-driven shift, not a law.

expression.glossEn: Would you like coffee? (du, not a title)

titleEn: Sisu: the Finnish word for continuing when continuing makes no sense
facts: Sisu names determination in the face of hopeless odds, and it is used for winter repairs, long illnesses and finishing a bad year's harvest.
Finnish speakers use it as a compliment but also as a warning, because too much sisu can mean refusing help that is needed.
The word became a marketing slogan and a national brand, and Finnish researchers have noted its overuse in tourism copy.
Sisu is not the same as happiness or optimism; it describes endurance without a promise of reward.
The concept spread into English through Finnish-American communities and re-entered Finland as an export product.
exampleEn: A Finnish farmer whose roof collapses in February repairs it in the dark and calls the effort sisu, then tells his son not to inherit the habit because the roof should have been fixed in autumn.
qualificationEn: Sisu is a national self-image rather than a measurable trait, and Finns often use it ironically; Swedish-speaking Finns and newer immigrant communities relate to it differently.

titleEn: Icelandic names: why the phone book is sorted by first name
facts: Most Icelanders have a patronymic or matronymic rather than a family name, so a son of Jón is Jónsson and a daughter is Jónsdóttir.
Surnames change every generation, which is why the Icelandic phone book is sorted by first name.
People are addressed by first name in almost every setting, including with teachers and officials, and surnames are rarely used vocatively.
Iceland keeps a naming committee that must approve new first names, and names must fit Icelandic grammar and gender conventions.
Matronymics have become more common as a deliberate choice, so siblings can carry different surnames from each other.
exampleEn: An Icelandic student meeting a bank clerk calls her by first name and never learns her surname; when the clerk's son is registered at school he is listed under his own first name plus his father's name.
qualificationEn: Family names do exist in Iceland, especially among families with foreign ancestry and some established lineages; the naming committee's rules are debated, and immigrant names are treated separately.

region: Nationwide, strongest in Dublin and the west
titleEn: Craic: the Irish word for talk that is worth the journey
facts: Craic means enjoyable conversation, news and atmosphere, and the question What's the craic? asks both what is happening and how you are.
The word was borrowed into English from Irish (or from northern English dialect) and became a marker of Irish identity in the 1990s.
Having the craic is an activity rather than a mood, and it is judged by the quality of the talk rather than the venue.
The spelling craic was promoted in the 1960s and 1970s by Dublin publicans, and the older English form crack still appears in Scotland.
Irish-language writers point out that spraoi is the native word for fun, and that craic came from English dialect before becoming a marker of Irishness.
exampleEn: An Irish host asks what's the craic before asking whether you want tea, and a flat answer about the weather ends the exchange faster than a bad joke about it would.
qualificationEn: Craic is semi-performative and heavily commercialised for tourists; not every Irish person uses it, and in Northern Ireland the word carries different political and social associations.

titleEn: Cwtch: the Welsh word for a hug that is also a safe place
facts: Cwtch can mean a cuddle, but also a cupboard or a small safe space, and the two meanings are linked rather than separate.
The verb form cwtchu is used for comforting a child, and the noun can name the place where something is kept safe.
Welsh pronunciation puts the stress on the first syllable and the final ch is the same sound as in Scottish loch.
The word appears in Welsh-language children's books and in English-language marketing in Wales as a symbol of national warmth.
Welsh-medium education has increased the number of young speakers, and cwtch is one of the words they carry into English conversation.
exampleEn: A Cardiff mother tells her crying son to come for a cwtch, and the same word is stencilled on a cafe door meaning the snug back room where regulars sit.
qualificationEn: Welsh speakers are concentrated in north-west and south Wales, and many Welsh people do not speak Welsh; using cwtch in English is a choice that signals Welshness rather than fluency.

titleEn: Tu and usted: Spanish politeness that is moving down the age scale
facts: Spanish chooses between tu (familiar) and usted (formal, grammatically third person), and the verb forms differ: tu tienes versus usted tiene.
Usted is used with strangers, older people and in service encounters, but Spanish doctors and teachers increasingly use tu with adult patients and students.
In Spain usted has receded among young people, while in much of Latin America it remains standard with strangers.
The plural adds another layer: vosotros is the familiar plural in Spain, while Latin America uses ustedes for both familiar and formal address.
Choosing tu too soon can feel presumptuous; choosing usted with a peer can feel like a deliberate rebuke.
exampleEn: A Madrid shop assistant in her twenties calls a customer of forty tu and the customer's father usted in the same minute, adjusting mid-sentence without any loss of fluency.
qualificationEn: Usage varies by country, region, class and generation: Colombian and Costa Rican speakers use usted very broadly, and Argentine Spanish uses vos instead of tu, so no single rule covers the Spanish-speaking world.

titleEn: Sobremesa: the part of the meal that happens after the food
facts: Sobremesa means over the table: the conversation that continues after eating, with coffee, dessert or nothing at all.
Restaurants tolerate it, and in southern Spain a lunch can run until mid-afternoon without the table being cleared.
The custom is tied to late eating hours and to social life being scheduled around the table rather than after it.
Business talk often happens during sobremesa, which is why Spanish meetings may begin with lunch and end with an agreement.
Younger urban Spaniards report shorter sobremesas because of work schedules, and takeaway culture is changing the pattern.
exampleEn: A Seville family finishes lunch at three and leaves the table at five, with the plates pushed aside and the conversation moving through football, a cousin's operation and a house purchase.
qualificationEn: Sobremesa length varies by region, age and work schedule; in Madrid and Barcelona weekday lunches are often short, and tourism has changed restaurant expectations in city centres.

expression.glossEn: the talk at the table after the meal

titleEn: Saudade: the Portuguese word for missing something that may not come back
facts: Saudade names a longing for someone or something absent, and it can be sweet as well as painful rather than purely sad.
It is used for places, people, past periods and even for a feeling the speaker cannot name, which is why dictionaries struggle with it.
The word is central to fado lyrics, where it is performed rather than explained, and singers rarely gloss it for foreigners.
Portuguese grammar makes the feeling relational: ter saudade de alguem is to have longing of someone, not to be sad in general.
Brazilian Portuguese uses it at least as much as European Portuguese, and the meaning shifts from homesickness to affectionate nostalgia.
exampleEn: A Lisbon taxi driver playing fado says he has saudade of the neighbourhood he grew up in, although it is twenty minutes away and he still visits his mother there every Sunday.
qualificationEn: Saudade is a national cliche as well as a word, and Portuguese speakers use it casually without the literary weight foreigners attach to it; the Brazilian and European uses differ in tone.

titleEn: Ciao: the Italian goodbye that started as a servant's bow
facts: Ciao comes from the Venetian phrase s-ciao vostro, meaning I am your servant, and it entered general Italian from the Veneto in the nineteenth century.
It works for both hello and goodbye, but only informally; answering a formal greeting with ciao can be a deliberate intimacy move.
Northern Italians use ciao more broadly than southern Italians, and in some southern regions it still sounds regional or slightly cheeky.
The word spread internationally through fashion, film and tourism and now appears in German, Spanish and Japanese slang.
Its double duty as greeting and farewell is unusual among European interjections and reflects its origin in a gesture of deference, not a time of day.
exampleEn: A Milanese shopkeeper says ciao to a customer she has known for years and buongiorno to the next one, and the two greetings mark the difference between a relationship and a transaction.
qualificationEn: Ciao is informal and should not be used with officials, elderly strangers or in writing to a superior; regional usage differs, and the word's Venetian origin is often unknown to speakers.

region: Nationwide, stronger in Crete and the islands
titleEn: Filotimo: the Greek word for doing the right thing when nobody is watching
facts: Filotimo combines philos (friend) and timi (honour) and names a disposition to act generously and honourably without being asked.
It is used to praise someone who refuses payment, helps a stranger or protects a family's name, and it can also justify stubbornness.
The word appears on Greek tourism campaigns and in village speech, where it describes a person rather than an action.
Filotimo is often described as untranslatable, but its content overlaps with dignity, self-respect and social obligation at once.
The word is used across the Greek-speaking world, including Cyprus, where it carries the same mix of generosity and touchiness.
exampleEn: A Cretan tavern owner refuses money from a table of strangers who helped clear a road after a storm, saying only that it was filotimo, and the refusal ends the discussion.
qualificationEn: Filotimo is a national ideal rather than a description of everyday behaviour, and Greeks use it ironically about people who insist on doing things their own way; diaspora usage often simplifies it to hospitality.

titleEn: Da net: the Russian answer that says no and implies yes
facts: Da net (yes, no) is a common reply that begins with agreement and ends with refusal, and its meaning depends entirely on intonation.
With a falling tone it can mean no, firmly; with a rising continuation it can mean yes, but, which is how speakers introduce a qualification.
Russian also uses da net, navernoye (yes no, probably) to soften a refusal that the speaker is not certain about.
The particle -to and the word konechno (of course) add further layers, so a two-word answer can carry a whole negotiation.
Russian conversation tolerates disagreement more openly than many northern European registers, and a flat no is not necessarily rude.
exampleEn: A Moscow colleague asked whether a deadline is realistic answers da net, and the project manager hears that the deadline is impossible but the team will try, which is exactly what the two words were doing.
qualificationEn: Intonation patterns vary by region and generation, and written da net loses the tone that makes it intelligible; younger Russians online often replace it with emoji or a dash.

titleEn: Pan and pani: Polish politeness that speaks about you, not to you
facts: Polish formal address uses pan (sir) and pani (madam) with third-person verbs: Czy moglby Pan powtorzyc? (could you repeat, sir).
The pronoun ty is reserved for friends, family, children and sometimes colleagues, and switching to it is a negotiated step.
The third-person construction keeps a grammatical distance even when the two people are standing close together.
In shops and offices pan or pani plus a first name is increasingly common, a compromise between formality and friendliness.
The same pan/pani system appears in Czech and Slovak, but Polish uses it more heavily in service encounters and in email.
exampleEn: A Warsaw student emails a lecturer with Szanowny Panie plus the title and third-person verbs, then signs off with a first name, because the opening must stay formal even when the closing is warm.
qualificationEn: Usage differs between generations and regions: western Poland and big cities switch to ty faster, and many workplaces use first names while keeping pan in customer contact.

titleEn: Tegezes and magazas: Hungarian's two machines for the same sentence
facts: Hungarian distinguishes tegezes (familiar te) from magazas (formal maga or on), and the verb endings change with each.
The formal form uses third-person verb endings for a second-person addressee, so the grammar keeps a step of distance.
On is the older, more distant form used with officials and in rural settings, while maga is common in cities and can sound slightly cold.
Switching from maga to te is offered by the older or senior person, often with szabad tegezodnom? (may I use te).
Hungarian is agglutinative, so the polite ending is a suffix rather than a separate pronoun, and dropping it changes the whole sentence.
exampleEn: A Budapest doctor asks a patient in his sixties whether he may use te; the patient agrees, and the consultation continues with different verb endings for both of them.
qualificationEn: Maga can feel offensive to some older Hungarians who prefer on, and usage varies by region and generation; diaspora Hungarian often preserves older formal patterns.

region: Serbia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro
titleEn: One language, four names: how Serbo-Croatian split into standards
facts: Serbo-Croatian was the common standard of Yugoslavia, and since the 1990s Croatia, Serbia, Bosnia and Montenegro have each cultivated a national standard.
The standards differ in vocabulary and in a few grammatical choices: Serbian prefers sta for what, Croatian sto, and Bosnian uses both.
Pronunciation differs too: ekavian (mleko, milk) in Serbia and ijekavian (mlijeko) in Croatia, Bosnia and Montenegro.
Scripts are political as well as practical: Cyrillic dominates in Serbia, Latin in Croatia, and both are used in Bosnia.
Most speakers understand each other without effort, which makes the division a case of what linguists call pluricentric standardisation rather than four separate languages.
exampleEn: A Belgrade journalist and a Zagreb journalist interview each other without interpreters, then argue for ten minutes about whether the word for train station is a Serbian or Croatian form.
qualificationEn: National standards are real institutions with school curricula and dictionaries, and calling the language one thing or another is politically loaded; regional and generational variation is larger than the standard differences suggest.

titleEn: Surzhyk: the Ukrainian-Russian mix that has no official name on a form
facts: Surzhyk is the mixed Ukrainian-Russian speech common in central and eastern Ukraine, with Ukrainian grammar and Russian vocabulary, or the reverse.
The word originally meant flour mixed from different grains and carries a pejorative charge that speakers dispute.
Surzhyk arose through urbanisation and Soviet-era Russification, when villagers moved to Russian-speaking cities and children grew up between the two languages.
It is not a single variety: the mix differs from Kyiv to Kharkiv to Odesa, and the proportions change with the speaker's generation.
Since 2014 and especially 2022, many speakers have deliberately shifted towards Ukrainian, and surzhyk has become a marker of a particular generation rather than a default.
exampleEn: A Kyiv market seller switches from Ukrainian to Russian for a price and back to surzhyk for a joke, and a customer from Lviv understands everything while noticing each shift.
qualificationEn: Surzhyk is stigmatised in some schools and celebrated in others, and census categories do not capture it; attitudes have changed sharply since the full-scale invasion, with strong regional variation.

titleEn: Grüezi: the Swiss greeting that marks the border before the border does
facts: Grüezi (often Grüezi mitenand for a group) is the standard Swiss German greeting, used with strangers and in shops.
It is shortened from Gott gruezi, may God greet you, and the form is rare in Germany, where Hallo or Guten Tag dominate.
Swiss German is used for speech and Standard German for writing, so the same person reads the news in one language and greets the baker in another.
The language border is sharp: crossing into French-speaking Switzerland replaces Gruezi with Bonjour, and bilingual cities such as Biel switch constantly.
Swiss German dialects differ enough that a Basel speaker and a Bern speaker may switch to Standard German to be understood.
exampleEn: A Zurich hiker greets every passer-by with a Gruezi, and by the time she reaches the Bernese Oberland she is answering Gruezi with Gruezi even though her own dialect has become hard for locals to place.
qualificationEn: Greeting customs vary between cantons and between city and village; younger Swiss use Hallo more, and Swiss German is a family of dialects rather than a single spoken standard.

region: Northern Albania, Kosovo and North Macedonia
titleEn: Besa: the Albanian promise that outranks a written contract
facts: Besa means word of honour and pledged faith, and a person who keeps besa is trusted with money, safety and secrets.
The concept is embedded in the Kanun customary code, which regulates hospitality, blood feuds and the protection of guests.
During the Second World War, besa was invoked to protect Jewish refugees in Albania, and the story is part of national memory and public commemoration.
Besa can bind a whole family, not just an individual, and breaking it damages the family's standing rather than the speaker's alone.
Albanian has a verb, beboj, and phrases such as e kam besa (I have pledged it), which show that the concept is grammatical as well as moral.
exampleEn: A Kosovo shopkeeper lets a stranger take goods on credit because the man gave his besa; when the payment arrives a month later there is no receipt and nobody expected one.
qualificationEn: Besa is an ideal drawn from customary law, and modern Albania and Kosovo rely on courts and contracts; urban and diaspora Albanians often describe it as a family value rather than a working rule.

region: Europe and the Balkans, with diaspora in the Americas
titleEn: Romani: a language with no home state and many names for itself
facts: Romani is an Indo-Aryan language spoken across Europe, and its varieties differ enough that some are not mutually intelligible.
Speakers call themselves Roma, Sinti, Kale or Manouche depending on region, and the language name follows the community rather than a country.
The language has no official state, and standardisation is contested because codifying one variety would privilege one community.
Romani has been written in Latin, Cyrillic and other scripts, and a common orthography remains a political project rather than a fact.
Many Roma are multilingual, using the majority language at school and Romani at home, and some varieties are now endangered by pressure to assimilate.
exampleEn: A Romani family in Transylvania speaks one variety at home, switches to Romanian at the clinic and to Hungarian at the market, and the children answer their grandmother in Romani while playing in Romanian.
qualificationEn: Roma are not a single community, and estimates of speakers vary widely; some groups avoid identifying as Roma because of discrimination, and Romani is recognised as a minority language in only some European states.

titleEn: How are you: the American greeting that is really a handshake
facts: How are you? functions as a greeting rather than a medical question, and the expected answer is Good, how are you? or another short formula.
A stranger asking on the street may not want an answer, and a long honest reply can break the ritual by turning it into a conversation.
Regional variants do the same work: How's it going?, What's up? in New York, Howdy in Texas, and You all right? in parts of the South.
The answer pretty good hedges more than good, while fine can signal that something is wrong without saying so.
Service workers are trained to ask and keep moving, so the exchange often happens while both people are walking in opposite directions.
exampleEn: A New Yorker asks a colleague how are you while already turning towards the lift, and the colleague answers good, thanks without breaking stride; both have exchanged recognition, not information.
qualificationEn: The ritual is not uniquely American and varies by region, class and setting: in the US South the exchange may genuinely open into family news, and in a doctor's waiting room the question is literal again.

titleEn: Bless your heart: the Southern phrase that can be sympathy or the opposite
facts: The phrase is literally a blessing, and in older rural usage it is sincere sympathy after an illness, a bereavement or bad luck.
Said with a certain tone, it can also mark someone as foolish or naive while keeping the speaker's manners intact.
It often closes a conversation about a third person's bad decision, letting the speaker judge without stating a judgement.
The expression spread nationally through television and the internet, where it is now usually used self-consciously as a meme.
Southerners disagree about how often it is meant unkindly, and the ambiguity is precisely what makes it useful.
exampleEn: A Georgia aunt hears that a nephew has bought a boat he cannot afford and says bless his heart; everyone at the table understands the verdict, and nobody has been criticised out loud.
qualificationEn: Meaning depends on tone, relationship and region, and many Southerners use it only sincerely; outside the South the ironic reading often dominates, which is why transplants misread it.

region: Nationwide, strongest in the South and in cities
titleEn: He be working: the habitual be that English usually lacks
facts: African-American Vernacular English marks habitual action with be, so he be working means he works regularly rather than he is working now.
The variety also marks remote past with been, as in I been knew, and allows zero copula in sentences such as she nice.
These are systematic aspect distinctions rather than omissions, and speakers switch between AAVE and Standard English depending on setting.
Many features come from Southern English and from contact with West African languages during slavery, and the variety has its own grammar and narrative tradition.
The habitual be is spreading into internet English and into other dialects through music, which linguists track as borrowing rather than error.
exampleEn: A Detroit teacher hears a student say he be late and understands that the boy is routinely late, not late today, so she asks about the pattern rather than the morning.
qualificationEn: AAVE is not a single uniform variety, and its features vary by region, age and class; writing it in dialogue can be respectful or caricature depending on who is writing and why.

titleEn: Eh: the Canadian tag that asks you to agree without arguing
facts: Eh is a tag particle placed at the end of a statement to invite agreement, as in nice day, eh? or you're coming, eh?.
It also marks narrative and shared knowledge, and it can stand alone as a request to repeat something.
The particle exists in other Englishes, including New Zealand and parts of Britain, but Canadian English uses it with distinctive frequency and function.
Canadians themselves treat eh as a mild stereotype, and many younger urban speakers use it less than the stereotype suggests.
Canadian English also has recognisable vowel patterns, such as Canadian raising in about and house, which are harder to parody than eh.
exampleEn: A Toronto colleague ends a meeting summary with so we're agreed, eh?, and the room answers with nods rather than words, because the particle has already done the asking.
qualificationEn: Frequency and function vary by region, age and first language; francophone Canadians use a different set of tags, and the eh stereotype is exported more than it is performed.

titleEn: Bonjour, hi: the Montreal greeting that refuses to guess your language
facts: Montreal shop staff often open with Bonjour, hi! to signal that service is available in French and English without asking which one you prefer.
The greeting is a practical solution to a language-political problem, because guessing wrong can insult a customer in either direction.
Quebec's Charter of the French Language requires French to be the normal language of commerce, and the bilingual greeting sits at the edge of that rule.
In 2017 the National Assembly passed a motion urging merchants to greet with bonjour alone, and the debate became a small national controversy.
In Quebec French, bonjour also serves as goodbye, unlike in France, so the same word opens and closes the transaction.
exampleEn: A clerk in a Plateau shop says bonjour, hi to everyone who enters, then continues in whichever language the customer answers, switching twice in a minute without comment.
qualificationEn: Bonjour, hi is common in Montreal but less so in Quebec City and rural regions, and some francophones hear it as a refusal to commit to French; younger bilinguals use it casually.

titleEn: Mande: the Mexican pardon that literally means command me
facts: Mande comes from mandar (to command) and works as pardon?, what did you say? or at your service, especially when speaking to an elder.
It usually accompanies usted, so the deference is doubled: the younger speaker submits grammatically and lexically at once.
In Spain the same situation calls for como? or perdone, and mande in Spain sounds old-fashioned or Latin American.
Parents teach children to answer mande rather than que? because que? alone is considered abrupt.
The form survives strongly in central and southern Mexico and in Mexican-American communities in the United States.
exampleEn: A grandmother in Puebla says something from the kitchen, and her grandson answers mande? before he has even turned around, because the word is the reflex of respect rather than a request to repeat.
qualificationEn: Mande is regional and generational: northern Mexican speech uses it less, urban young people often say como? or mande? interchangeably, and in Spain the form is rare.

titleEn: Ahorita: the Mexican word that means now, soon or never
facts: Ahorita is the diminutive of ahora (now), and the diminutive makes the timing smaller, softer and less committal.
It can mean this instant, in a few minutes or at some unspecified future point, and tone plus gesture decide which.
Ahorita vengo (I'll be right back) is said by shopkeepers who may return in two minutes or twenty.
The word softens a refusal or a delay without stating either, which makes it useful in service encounters and family arguments.
Other Spanish-speaking countries use ahorita too, but Mexican Spanish has made it a near-universal conversational tool.
exampleEn: A Mexico City plumber says ahorita to three different customers in one morning: for the first it means within the hour, for the second this afternoon, and for the third he knows it means next week.
qualificationEn: Meaning depends entirely on context and relationship, and foreigners who take ahorita as now are routinely disappointed; northern and southern Mexican usage also differs in how far the delay stretches.

titleEn: La utz awach: the K'iche' greeting that asks about your face
facts: La utz awach? literally asks whether your face is good, and it is the ordinary K'iche' greeting rather than a formal formula.
The expected answer is utz, maltyox (good, thank you), and the exchange is often followed by a question about family or the harvest.
K'iche' is a Mayan language with ergative grammar, and it marks the subject of transitive and intransitive verbs differently.
Guatemala recognises 22 Mayan languages, and K'iche' is one of the largest, with roughly a million speakers and a written tradition going back to the Popol Vuh.
Many K'iche' speakers are bilingual in Spanish, and code-switching in markets mixes Spanish numbers and prices into K'iche' sentences.
exampleEn: A woman selling textiles in Chichicastenango greets a regular customer with la utz awach? and then quotes prices in Spanish, because numbers above twenty are usually borrowed.
qualificationEn: K'iche' has several dialects and spelling conventions, and urban Guatemalan Maya may speak mostly Spanish; the greeting varies between communities and between highland and coastal towns.

expression.glossEn: How are you? (is your face good?)

titleEn: Qanuippit: Inuktitut, polysynthesis and the snow-words hoax
facts: Inuktitut builds long words from a root plus many suffixes, so one word can carry what English spreads across a sentence.
The claim that Inuit languages have dozens or hundreds of words for snow began as a linguistic example and drifted into a hoax through repeated citation.
The confusion arises because polysynthetic languages productively combine a snow root with different suffixes, which makes counting words for snow meaningless.
Inuktitut is written in syllabics in Nunavut and in Latin letters in parts of Labrador and Greenland, and the syllabic system was adapted by missionaries in the nineteenth century.
Nunavut recognises Inuktitut and Inuinnaqtun as official languages alongside English and French, and Greenlandic is the official language of Greenland.
exampleEn: A Nunavut elder asked how many words Inuktitut has for snow answers by describing the difference between fresh snow, drifting snow and snow good for building, then says the question assumes words work the way English words do.
qualificationEn: Inuit languages form a dialect continuum, and what is true of Inuktitut in Nunavut may not hold in Greenland or Alaska; the number of fluent speakers varies sharply by community.

region: Jamaica, with diaspora in Britain, Canada and the US
titleEn: Wah gwaan: the Jamaican greeting built on West African grammar
facts: Jamaican Patois, or Patwa, is an English-based creole whose grammar retains West African patterns from Akan and Igbo speakers brought to the island.
Pronouns differ from English: mi covers I and me, yu covers you, and dem marks the plural, as in di pikni dem (the children).
The particle a marks progressive action, as in mi a go (I am going), and past tense is often carried by context rather than a verb ending.
Wah gwaan? (what is going on) is the everyday greeting, answered by mi de yah (I am here) or everything criss.
Patwa is used in music, church and family life while Standard Jamaican English dominates formal writing, a classic diglossia that Jamaicans navigate daily.
exampleEn: A Kingston bus conductor calls wah gwaan to a regular and gets mi de yah in reply, while the same man writes a job application in Standard English an hour later without noticing the switch.
qualificationEn: There is a continuum between Patwa and Standard Jamaican English rather than two separate languages, and urban middle-class speech sits in the middle; orthography is still debated and most writing uses English spelling.

expression.glossEn: what's going on? / how are you?

titleEn: Jeitinho: the Brazilian workaround that is admired and criticised at once
facts: Dar um jeitinho means finding a way around a rule or an obstacle, often through a personal contact or an improvised solution.
The same word describes harmless creativity, such as fixing a form at the last minute, and corruption, such as skipping a queue through a friend.
Brazilian Portuguese uses jeito for a knack or manner, so jeitinho literally means a little way of doing something.
The concept is often paired with the phrase voce sabe com quem esta falando? (do you know who you are talking to?), which invokes hierarchy instead of improvisation.
Sociologists treat jeitinho as a response to bureaucracy and inequality: when rules are slow and unequal, personal routes become rational.
exampleEn: A Sao Paulo office worker missing a document gets a colleague to phone the registry and have it released the same day, then calls the result a jeitinho and is proud of it.
qualificationEn: Jeitinho is a national self-description and contested: many Brazilians condemn it as corruption, and the term's approval depends on whether the workaround harms someone else.

region: Buenos Aires, Montevideo and the Pampas
titleEn: Vos sos: how the Rio de la Plata replaced tu with vos
facts: Rioplatense Spanish uses vos instead of tu for the familiar singular, with its own verb forms: vos sos, vos tenes, vos podes.
The vos paradigm comes from older Spanish, and it survived in the region while peninsular Spanish standardised tu.
Voseo carries its own imperatives, so veni (come) and decime (tell me) replace ven and dime.
In Buenos Aires and Montevideo vos is near-universal among all classes, and using tu can sound foreign or deliberately affected.
Other Spanish-speaking regions also use vos, including parts of Colombia, Central America and Paraguay, but with different forms and social meanings from the Rio de la Plata.
exampleEn: An Argentine teacher asks a Spanish exchange student vos sabes? and the student answers in tu, and the mismatch is not a misunderstanding but a small map of where each of them learned Spanish.
qualificationEn: Voseo varies by country: Central American and Colombian voseo differ in form and register, and in Argentina the pronoun is universal while the verb endings still vary regionally.

titleEn: Che: the two-letter Argentine word that starts half the sentences in Buenos Aires
facts: Che is an interjection used to call or address someone, roughly hey or mate, as in che, que haces?.
It appears mid-sentence as an attention marker, so a bus driver can say che, subi at the back without looking at anyone.
The word is often linked to Guarani che (I, me), though its path into Argentine Spanish is debated by linguists.
Ernesto Guevara was nicknamed Che by Cuban and other Latin American comrades because of his Argentine speech, and the name became global.
Che also exists as a Valencian interjection of complaint, which is unrelated in origin and usually pronounced differently.
exampleEn: Two Buenos Aires friends greet each other with che and continue with che three more times in a two-minute conversation, and the word marks attention rather than address.
qualificationEn: Che is widespread in Argentina and Uruguay but marked as Argentine elsewhere; in Paraguay it is understood but not native, and overusing it as a foreigner sounds like imitation.

titleEn: Si po: the Chilean particle that ends arguments and sentences
facts: Po is a Chilean particle shortened from pues, and it attaches to yes, no and other words: si po, no po, ya po.
It adds emphasis, impatience or warmth depending on tone, and it can turn a bare si into an unmistakably Chilean answer.
Chilean Spanish also drops final s and consonant clusters, so como estas? becomes como estai? and para becomes pa.
The word cachar (to get it, to understand) came into Chilean Spanish from English catch and now has its own Chilean meanings.
Po is stigmatised in formal writing and school, but it is normal in speech across classes and appears in advertising aimed at young Chileans.
exampleEn: A Santiago shopkeeper answers si po to a customer who asks whether the shop is open, and the particle conveys both yes and mild surprise that the question needed asking.
qualificationEn: Po is general in Chile but rare elsewhere in Latin America, and its intensity varies by class and region; formal writing removes it, so learners meet it only in speech and social media.

region: Andean highlands (Cusco, Puno, La Paz, Otavalo)
titleEn: Allillanchu: Quechua and the evidence suffixes that say how you know
facts: Quechua is a family of related languages spoken by several million people in Peru, Bolivia and Ecuador and is official in all three states.
It is agglutinative and adds suffixes for who did what to whom, so word order carries less weight than in Spanish.
Quechua marks information source: a suffix can say that the speaker saw something directly, and another that it was reported or inferred.
Allillanchu? asks whether someone is well, and the answer allillanmi includes the direct-evidence suffix, which claims the speaker knows from experience.
The Inca moral triad ama sua, ama llulla, ama quella (do not steal, do not lie, do not be lazy) is still quoted in Quechua and Spanish across the Andes.
exampleEn: A Cusco market seller describing a rumour adds the reported-evidence suffix, and a local customer understands that she did not witness the event although the Spanish translation she gives contains no such warning.
qualificationEn: Quechua is a family rather than one language, and Cusco, Ayacucho and Ecuadorian varieties differ substantially; written standards and orthographies remain contested, and many speakers are bilingual in Spanish.

titleEn: Kamisaraki: Aymara, the language where the past may be in front of you
facts: Kamisaraki? is the everyday Aymara greeting, answered waliki (fine), and it is used across the Bolivian and Peruvian altiplano.
Aymara is an official language of Bolivia alongside Spanish and the other indigenous languages recognised in the 2009 constitution.
Like Quechua, Aymara marks evidentiality on the verb, so a speaker states whether an event was seen, heard or inferred.
Linguists have argued that Aymara places the past in front of the speaker and the future behind, because the past is known and visible while the future is not.
Aymara and Quechua share vocabulary through centuries of contact, but they belong to different language families and are not mutually intelligible.
exampleEn: An El Alto bus driver points forward when talking about his grandfather's village and backward when talking about next year's plans, and the gesture matches the verb forms he is using.
qualificationEn: The time-metaphor claim is based on gesture studies and is debated, and it does not mean Aymara speakers experience time differently; urban Aymara speech is heavily mixed with Spanish.

region: Nationwide, especially Asuncion and the countryside
titleEn: Mba'eichapa: Paraguayan Guarani and the mixed speech that holds the country together
facts: Guarani is co-official with Spanish in Paraguay, and a large majority of the population speaks it, including many people who do not identify as indigenous.
Mba'eichapa? is the ordinary how are you, answered ipora (fine), and it is used by presidents and bus drivers alike.
Jopara is the mixed Guarani-Spanish speech of Asuncion, in which Spanish nouns and verbs are fitted into Guarani grammar and pronunciation.
Guarani is agglutinative and nasal-vowel rich, and it distinguishes inclusive and exclusive we, a distinction Spanish lacks.
Paraguay made Guarani official in the 1992 constitution, and it is the only country in the Americas where an indigenous language is spoken by a majority.
exampleEn: A Asuncion student explains a phone problem in Guarani, inserts the Spanish word for signal and continues in Guarani, and her mother understands every word without noticing the switch.
qualificationEn: Guarani and jopara are not the same thing, and purists object to the mixing; urban middle-class families may speak more Spanish at home, and indigenous Guarani communities have their own varieties.

titleEn: Fa waka: Suriname's creole that most of the country actually speaks
facts: Sranan Tongo is an English-based creole and the main lingua franca of Suriname, although Dutch is the official language.
Fa waka? (how is it walking) is the everyday greeting, and mi de (I am here) or bun (good) answers it.
Its pronouns are mi, yu and a for I, you and he or she, and plural is marked by den, as in den sma (the people).
The language formed on seventeenth-century plantations from English with Portuguese, Dutch and West African contributions, and words such as pikin (child) probably come from Portuguese.
Sranan is used in radio, churches and politics, and a standard orthography was adopted in 1986, though Dutch remains the language of school and law.
exampleEn: Two colleagues in Paramaribo greet each other with fa waka and continue in Sranan, then switch to Dutch the moment a written document appears, because the paper belongs to the other language.
qualificationEn: Sranan is not the only creole in Suriname, and Sarnami, Javanese and Maroon languages are also spoken; Dutch dominates formal domains, and spelling practices still vary in informal writing.

region: Nationwide, strongest in the North Island
titleEn: Kia ora: the Māori greeting that became the country's hello
facts: Kia ora means be well and works as hello, thank you and cheers, and it is now used by most New Zealanders in English conversation.
Formal Māori greeting distinguishes tēnā koe (to one person) and tēnā koutou (to three or more), and kia ora can close a speech as well as open one.
Vowel length is written with macrons and changes meaning: māori (ordinary) and Māori (the people) are different words, not one with a typo.
Te reo Māori became an official language of New Zealand in 1987, after decades in which children were punished for speaking it at school.
The kōhanga reo language-nest movement, started in 1982, put Māori-speaking elders into preschools and is credited with halting the language's decline among young children.
exampleEn: A Wellington bus driver says kia ora to every passenger and gets a kia ora back from about half of them, including people who speak no other Maori word.
qualificationEn: Māori usage varies widely: some New Zealanders use kia ora as a genuine greeting, others as decoration, and fluency is concentrated in specific communities and age groups.

titleEn: Whakapapa: the genealogy that is recited rather than researched
facts: Whakapapa means to place in layers, and it names both a genealogy and the act of reciting it.
A whakapapa connects a person to ancestors, land, rivers and mountains, and it establishes rights and obligations rather than only family history.
Formal recitation happens on the marae, where a speaker names ancestors and landmarks to locate the visiting group.
The recitation is shortened or expanded according to the occasion, so the same person may give a two-minute or a twenty-minute version.
The term has moved into wider New Zealand English, where people speak of the whakapapa of a policy, a building or a gene.
exampleEn: A young Maori researcher introducing herself at a hui names her mountain, river and ancestor before her university, and the room now knows how she is connected to the people already seated.
qualificationEn: Whakapapa knowledge is held by particular families and is not always public, and misuse of the term for non-Maori genealogy is criticised; urban Maori who grew up outside their marae may be learning their own whakapapa as adults.

region: Samoa, with communities in New Zealand, Australia and the US
titleEn: Talofa: Samoan greeting and the fa'a Samoa obligations behind it
facts: Talofa is the ordinary Samoan greeting, and talofa lava is addressed to a group.
Fa'a Samoa, the Samoan way, organises life around the aiga (extended family), the matai (titled chief) and service (tautua) to both.
Respect is encoded in language: a separate vocabulary is used for chiefs and for formal oratory, and ordinary words have chiefly equivalents.
The 'ava ceremony formalises meetings with a drink made from the kava root, and the order of serving mirrors rank within the village.
Migration to New Zealand and the United States means many Samoan families maintain fa'a Samoa through church, remittances and village obligations from a distance.
exampleEn: A Samoan family in Auckland sends money and tinned food for a village funeral, and the matai thanks them by name in a speech that treats the overseas branch as physically present.
qualificationEn: Fa'a Samoa is an ideal as well as a practice, and urban Samoans, migrants and younger generations negotiate it differently; the chiefly system and land tenure are also internally contested.

region: Tonga, with diaspora in New Zealand, Australia and the US
titleEn: Malō e lelei: Tongan greeting inside a language of rank
facts: Malō e lelei is the standard Tongan greeting, and malo alone also means thank you.
Formal Tongan uses a chiefly register with separate vocabulary for many everyday words, so a speech addressed to nobles differs in word choice and not only in tone.
Society is organised around 'eiki (chiefs) and tu'a (commoners), and language marks the relationship in vocabulary choice and in the use of the definite accent.
The kava circle, with its own seating order and speech formulas, is where formal Tongan oratory is performed.
Tongan is a Polynesian language with a definitive accent, so stress placement can mark a noun as definite, a feature rare among its neighbours.
exampleEn: A Tongan student in Auckland addresses an older visiting relative with chiefly vocabulary and a different word for eat, and the choice of word does more social work than the sentence's content.
qualificationEn: Rank-based vocabulary is strongest in formal and rural settings, and diaspora Tongans often simplify it; commoners and nobles negotiate the register differently, and the monarchy's role is politically contested.

region: Nationwide, strongest in Bau and the main islands
titleEn: Bula: the Fijian hello that is a wish for life
facts: Bula means life or health, and it is the standard hello between strangers, shopkeepers and colleagues; bula vinaka adds good.
The word is used so often that visitors report hearing it from every doorway, and it survives in Fiji English as a greeting in its own right.
Fijian is an Austronesian language with several dialects, and the Bauan dialect became the standard through nineteenth-century mission and colonial use.
The 1997 constitution named English, Fijian and Hindustani as official languages, and the 2013 constitution keeps English as the working language while requiring translation into iTaukei and Hindi.
Respect in Fijian is shown through the use of titles and through the avoidance of direct contradiction in village meetings.
exampleEn: A visitor walking through a Suva market is greeted with bula by every stallholder in turn, and answering bula back is enough to be treated as a customer rather than a stranger.
qualificationEn: Fijian is not the first language of Indo-Fijians, who may greet with namaste or hello, and urban Fiji English mixes all three communities; village protocol differs from town manners.

titleEn: Aloha: the Hawaiian word that is a greeting, a feeling and a land ethic
facts: Aloha covers hello, goodbye, love and compassion, and aloha aina extends the idea to care for the land.
Hawaiian has thirteen letters including the glottal stop written as an okina and long vowels written with a macron, and both change meaning.
A 1896 law made English the required medium of instruction in Hawaii's schools, which pushed Hawaiian out of the classroom and led to punishment for speaking it.
Hawaiian became an official state language in 1978, and the Pūnana Leo preschool movement, founded in 1984, taught it to a new generation.
Hawaiian words have entered global English, sometimes stripped of their meaning, which is why the state promotes correct spelling and pronunciation.
exampleEn: A Honolulu teacher opens a staff meeting with aloha and then explains that the word obliges the meeting to behave differently, because it names a relationship rather than a greeting.
qualificationEn: Aloha is a commodity in tourism advertising as well as a living concept, and Native Hawaiian communities differ on how it should be used by businesses; spelling without the okina and macrons is common but contested.

region: Nationwide, especially urban centres and the coast
titleEn: Wantok: the Tok Pisin word that turns a shared language into a duty
facts: Wantok combines wantaim (together) and tok (talk or language), and names someone who speaks the same language or belongs to the same clan.
The wantok system obliges people to help relatives with money, housing and jobs, and it functions as social security where the state is weak.
Papua New Guinea has more than eight hundred languages, so Tok Pisin and Hiri Motu became the practical lingua francas and Tok Pisin is now an official language.
Tok Pisin began as a plantation pidgin in the nineteenth century and expanded into radio, parliament and newspapers.
Critics blame wantok for nepotism in public hiring, while defenders point out that the same network is what people rely on when formal services fail.
exampleEn: A Port Moresby nurse receives six requests for school fees from wantoks in one month and pays two, knowing that refusing all six would end the support she may need herself.
qualificationEn: Wantok obligations vary between highland and coastal societies and between urban and village life, and the term is used both warmly and accusingly; not every shared-language acquaintance counts as a wantok.

titleEn: Ngurra: the Warlpiri word for country that also names who you are related to
facts: Ngurra means camp, home or country, and it carries obligations to look after that place and the people connected to it.
Warlpiri kinship divides people into categories with expected behaviour, including avoidance relationships with certain in-laws.
The language is ergative and has free word order, so case endings rather than position show who did what to whom.
Warlpiri has been taught bilingually in Northern Territory schools, and the Warlpiri Literature Production Centre at Yuendumu produced books and dictionaries in the language.
Like many Australian languages, Warlpiri lost speakers through mission and assimilation policies, and revitalisation work now runs through community-controlled schools and media.
exampleEn: A Warlpiri man driving past a waterhole slows without being asked, because ngurra is not scenery but a relationship that requires acknowledgement.
qualificationEn: Warlpiri is one of many Australian languages with distinct kinship systems, and community protocols about who may speak for country are not public; bilingual education has been cut and restored unevenly.
